title: A Glance of Nectar
story:
The summer had grown heavy over Vrindavan, and the heat lay on everything like a weight. The rains were still far off, and the grass had begun to brown at the edges; the river alone still ran cool and inviting. Week after week the hot season had worn on without relief; even the shade at midday lay heavy and still. The heat fell hardest on the ones who could not rest — the cattle and the boys who watched them, out in the pasture from morning to evening. That day, burning with thirst, they came down together to the bank of the Yamuna. They had drunk from the river a hundred times and never thought twice, for it had always been sweet and clear. They did not know what had come to live in its depths.

They bent to the water and drank, boys and cattle together, glad of the coolness. The cattle pressed in at the shallows while the boys drank from their cupped hands, and the river took them all in. But the water was no longer what it had been. The venom did its work quickly and completely. One after another they fell — the boys, the cows, the calves — their minds struck down as if by the hand of fate itself, and they lay lifeless beside the water they had just drunk. There was no warning, and no one left standing to raise a cry. The river went on running, bright and untroubled, and the fallen lay still beside it.

Then Krishna came and saw them as they lay. He had been somewhere among the groves when the water did its work, moving through Vrindavana as he was always moving through it, and he had come back to the river to find them. He was the master of every yoga, the master even of the masters, and what had befallen them was, to him, a thing easily undone. Power with him was not a struggle, and mercy with him was not an effort. He simply looked at them — a single glance that showered nectar like rain — and where the poison had reached, life came flowing back. It took no time at all; it took the time of a single look.

The cowherds stirred and rose, and the cattle climbed to their feet beside them, and one by one they came back to themselves at the water's edge, as if waking from a sleep that held no dreams. Struck down by what seemed the hand of fate, they had been given back by what they could only call grace. Colour returned to their faces, and strength to their limbs, and the terror of what had happened drained away as though it had never been. Memory returned with breath, and it came back whole — the walk through the parched pasture, the sight of the river, the first cool mouthful, and then nothing, until the light of his looking. The interval between the two was simply gone, as though it had never been lived. They looked at one another, and then at Krishna standing over them, and they understood, without being told, what had happened. This was no ordinary recovery, and no medicine had done it. It was the mercy of Govinda, arriving in a look.

They did not make speeches of thanks. There was nothing to say to a glance that had undone death itself. They only understood, in that quiet way that needs no words, that the one who walked among them as a cowherd had reached down and gathered them back from the dark. They rose from the water's edge and stood on the ground where they had fallen, the river running past them as though nothing had happened here at all.
reflection: The verses are almost austere, and that is their power: no battle, no incantation, only a look. Krishna's compassion here is effortless, and the cowherds' silent understanding — that they had been raised by grace alone — is the true heart of the episode.
next_story_tease: And having seen what the venom could do, Krishna turned at last toward the deep pool itself, to put an end to it.
hero_scene: Krishna standing over the fallen cowherds and cattle by the water's edge, looking at them with calm, as they stir and rise back to life around him.
